value.overview: The Mallard is a widespread dabbling duck found across much of the Northern Hemisphere. It is adaptable and uses natural wetlands, ponds, lakes, slow-moving rivers, reservoirs, estuaries, and urban park waters. Males have a glossy green head, narrow white neck ring, chestnut breast, gray body, and yellow bill. Females are mottled brown with an orange-and-dark bill. The species is also the main wild ancestor of most domestic ducks.
value.classification: The Mallard belongs to the family Anatidae and order Anseriformes. Its scientific name is Anas platyrhynchos. Several regional forms are recognized, and domestic ducks are largely descended from this species.
value.identification: This is a fairly large, heavy-bodied duck with a relatively broad bill and a blue or purple wing speculum bordered by white. The adult male is distinctive: the head and upper neck are iridescent green, separated from the chestnut breast by a white collar. The female is mottled buff and brown, with an orange bill marked by darker areas. In Costa Rica, unusual ducks should be compared carefully with native and more regularly occurring species, as Mallards are exceptionally uncommon there.
value.rangeHabitat: Mallards have a very broad native range across North America, Europe, Asia, and parts of North Africa. They occupy freshwater marshes, shallow lakes, ponds, flooded fields, quiet rivers, reservoirs, and occasionally brackish coastal wetlands. In Costa Rica, the species is not a regular or common component of the avifauna. It has been regarded as a rare to casual visitor, with historical records from Guanacaste and the Central Valley, including wintering birds near Turrialba. There is no reliable evidence of an established breeding population.
value.migrationStatus: Northern populations are often migratory, while many birds in milder regions remain year-round. In Costa Rica, the Mallard is best treated as an exceptionally rare or casual migrant and winter visitor rather than a regular seasonal species. Historical Costa Rican records are sparse, and recent occurrence appears very limited or undocumented.
value.breeding: Mallards usually breed near shallow freshwater, including marshes, lake margins, ponds, and slow streams. The female selects a concealed nest on the ground among grasses or other vegetation, sometimes at a considerable distance from water. She commonly lays a large clutch and alone incubates the eggs and leads the ducklings. Mallards can breed successfully in human-modified landscapes, but there are no reliable records indicating regular breeding by wild Mallards in Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: Mallards are opportunistic feeders. They eat seeds, aquatic plants, grasses, grains, and other plant material, along with insects, insect larvae, small mollusks, crustaceans, worms, and other small aquatic animals. They commonly feed by dabbling, tipping forward in shallow water while keeping the body afloat, and they also graze on land. Food availability and local habitat strongly influence their diet.
value.behavior: Mallards are generally social outside the breeding season and may gather in flocks or mix with other waterfowl. They spend much time resting on banks, mudflats, or floating vegetation and are strong, capable fliers. Pairs often form before the breeding season. Males give relatively quiet calls compared with females, whose familiar loud quacks are especially noticeable. They readily use artificial ponds and urban wetlands where suitable food and cover are available.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable overall, although trends vary among geographic populations and some regional populations may be declining.
